items.title: Plastic Piles Up: What Record Credit Card Balances Say About Household Budgets This Holiday Season
items.body:
Every November, the same two things collide: retailers roll out their biggest sales of the year, and households take stock of how much room they really have in their budgets. This year, the backdrop is a credit card debt load that has repeatedly set new records. Here is what the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's household debt data show, how card interest rates compare with earlier years, and what it all means for families heading into December.

## What the New York Fed data show

The New York Fed's Center for Microeconomic Data publishes the *Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit*, based on anonymized credit bureau records. It is one of the most widely cited gauges of how American households are borrowing.

Some of the broad patterns in recent reports:

- **Total household debt has climbed steadily.** In the third quarter of 2025, the report put total household debt at roughly $18.6 trillion, with mortgages making up the largest share.
- **Credit card balances sit above $1.2 trillion.** Balances crossed the $1 trillion mark in 2023 and have stayed above it since. Third-quarter 2025 figures were around $1.23 trillion.
- **Balances follow a seasonal rhythm.** Card balances usually dip in the first quarter, as people pay down holiday spending with tax refunds and bonuses, then rise through the year and peak around the end of the year.

Readers should check the most recent release on the New York Fed's website for current figures. The report is updated each quarter, and the numbers above are best read as a snapshot of the trend rather than the latest data point.

### Records in dollars are not always records in strain

A large share of the "record" headlines reflects simple arithmetic. Prices are higher than they were a few years ago, the population has grown, and incomes have risen in nominal terms. A bigger economy tends to carry bigger balances. Many cardholders also pay their bills in full every month, so a rising balance total does not automatically mean more households are in trouble.

The more telling signals sit underneath the headline number. These include the share of balances that are delinquent, how many borrowers carry a balance from month to month, and how fast new delinquencies are appearing.

## Delinquencies: where the stress shows up

The New York Fed also tracks how many borrowers fall behind on payments. Credit cards have consistently shown some of the highest delinquency transition rates among major debt types. In recent reports, a meaningful share of card balances moved into serious delinquency (90 or more days past due) within a year. That share is higher than the period just before the pandemic.

Younger borrowers and those in lower-income areas have generally shown more strain than older and higher-income groups. That uneven pattern matters. Overall averages can look manageable while a sizeable group of households is stretched thin.

## How card interest rates compare with past years

The cost of carrying a balance is where the story gets more pressing.

Federal Reserve data on interest rates for credit card accounts that are assessed interest have shown average rates in the low 20-percent range in recent years. Industry trackers report averages near 20 percent for new offers. By comparison:

- In the years after the 2008 financial crisis and through the 2010s, average card rates were typically in the low-to-mid teens.
- In 2021, when the Fed held its benchmark rate near zero, the average rate on interest-bearing accounts dipped to roughly 14 to 15 percent.
- After the Fed began raising rates sharply in 2022, card APRs followed. Most cards carry variable rates tied to the prime rate, so they adjust quickly when the Fed moves.

Card APRs have eased only slightly from their peak, even as the Fed has trimmed its benchmark rate. Because issuers set their own margins above the prime rate, a rate cut does not translate into a matching drop for cardholders.

### What a 21 percent APR means in practice

Consider a household carrying a $5,000 balance at an APR of about 21 percent. Making only a minimum payment, interest alone could add roughly $85 to $90 a month early on. The balance falls slowly, and the payoff stretches across many years. At a rate of 14 percent, the same balance would cost noticeably less in interest each month. The gap is small in any single month, but it compounds into hundreds or thousands of dollars over time.

## Why the holidays raise the stakes

Seasonal spending adds pressure at an already tight time. A few factors stand out:

1. **Holiday spending is large and concentrated.** The National Retail Federation and other groups have projected total holiday retail sales in the trillions of dollars in recent seasons. Much of that lands on cards over a few weeks.
2. **Buy now, pay later is part of the mix.** Installment plans can spread out costs, but they add another set of due dates on top of card payments.
3. **Prices remain a concern.** Even with inflation cooler than its 2022 peak, many households still feel the cumulative effect of higher costs for groceries, housing, insurance, and utilities. Less slack in the monthly budget leaves less room for gifts, travel, and hosting.
4. **January bills arrive later.** Holiday charges often appear on statements in December and January, which is when many families first see the full total.

## What families heading into December can do

None of this is a reason to panic, and none of it is personalized financial advice. But a few practical steps are widely recommended by consumer finance educators and nonprofit credit counselors:

- **Set a spending ceiling before shopping.** Decide on a total for gifts, food, and travel, and work backward to per-person amounts.
- **Know your APR and your balance.** Check your latest statement. If you already carry a balance, new holiday purchases will start accruing interest right away, because the grace period usually applies only when the balance is paid in full.
- **Prioritize the highest-rate debt.** Paying more than the minimum on the highest-APR card generally saves the most in interest.
- **Look at balance transfer or consolidation options carefully.** Introductory 0 percent offers can help, but transfer fees, the length of the promotional period, and the rate that applies afterward all matter.
- **Contact your issuer if you are struggling.** Some issuers offer hardship programs. Nonprofit credit counseling agencies, including members of the National Foundation for Credit Counseling, can also help build a repayment plan.
- **Use alerts and autopay for at least the minimum.** A missed payment can bring late fees and a penalty rate, and it can hurt your credit score.
- **Consider a smaller January.** A few gift-giving traditions, such as homemade gifts, shared experiences, or a set exchange, can lower the total without lowering the spirit of the season.

## The bigger picture

Record card balances are the product of several overlapping forces: higher prices, a larger economy, resilient consumer spending, and borrowing costs that remain well above their pandemic-era lows. For many households, the numbers are manageable. For others, particularly those carrying balances month to month at rates above 20 percent, the holiday season can deepen a cycle that is hard to escape.

The most useful way to read the New York Fed's data is not as a single alarming figure but as a set of trends. Balances are high, borrowing is expensive, and delinquencies are elevated in some groups. Families who go into December with a plan, a clear view of their rates, and a realistic limit are in the best position to start the new year without a heavy debt hangover.

*This article is for general informational purposes only and does not constitute financial, investment, or legal advice. Figures cited are drawn from publicly available reports from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the Federal Reserve and are approximate. Consult a qualified professional for guidance about your own situation.*

items.title: Mood vs. Money: Why Consumer Sentiment Surveys Often Miss What Shoppers Actually Do
items.body:
Every month, headlines announce that Americans are feeling gloomy about the economy. Every month, store traffic, card transactions and retail sales reports often tell a calmer story. The two can seem like they describe different countries. They don't. They measure different things, and understanding the gap can make you a better reader of economic news.

## What a consumer sentiment survey actually measures

The best-known gauge in the United States is the University of Michigan's Surveys of Consumers. A separate widely cited measure, the Consumer Confidence Index, comes from The Conference Board. Both are built from questionnaires sent to a sample of households.

The Michigan survey asks respondents a set of questions about:

- their own household's current finances compared with a year ago
- their expectations for their finances over the next year
- the outlook for the national economy over the short term and the next five years
- whether it is a good time to buy big-ticket items such as cars or appliances

Answers are converted into index scores. The survey also asks about expected inflation, which policymakers and analysts watch closely. The key point is that these are **opinions and expectations**, not records of purchases.

## How the surveys are built

A few design features shape what the numbers can and cannot tell you:

- **Sampling.** Pollsters contact a few hundred to a few thousand people and weight the results to match the broader population. Smaller samples carry a margin of error, so a small monthly move may be statistical noise rather than a real shift.
- **Method changes.** Over the years, many surveys have moved from telephone interviews to online panels. Response rates have fallen across the polling industry, and a change in method can change results, making long-run comparisons harder.
- **Question wording.** Questions that ask about "the economy" invite broad, emotional answers. Questions about personal finances tend to be more grounded.
- **Timing.** Surveys capture a snapshot over a few weeks. News events in that window can color responses.

None of this makes the surveys useless. It means they should be read as one input with known limits.

## Why words and wallets can diverge

Researchers have noted several reasons why what people say can differ from what they spend.

### 1. Prices are felt more than they are counted

Even when inflation slows, price *levels* remain higher than they were a few years ago. Many households judge the economy by the cost of groceries, rent, insurance and gas. A person can say conditions are poor because everyday items cost more, and still keep buying them, because they are necessities.

### 2. Spending is concentrated among a subset of households

Total retail sales are dominated by higher-income households, which hold most of the wealth and account for a large share of discretionary spending. If those households are comfortable thanks to rising stock portfolios or home values, aggregate spending can hold up even when lower-income households feel squeezed. A survey of all households and a dollar-weighted spending total are weighting people differently.

### 3. Mood is influenced by news and politics

Research has repeatedly found that sentiment readings can differ sharply depending on a respondent's political leanings and on the news they consume. Partisan swings in sentiment can occur without any change in people's actual finances. That makes the headline number a mix of economic experience and broader attitudes.

### 4. People spend on habit and need

Daily life continues regardless of mood. Rent is due, commutes happen, and children need shoes. Much consumer spending is routine, so it does not respond quickly to changes in outlook.

### 5. Credit and savings can bridge the gap

Households may feel pessimistic yet keep spending by drawing on savings, using credit cards, or using buy-now-pay-later plans. That can sustain spending for a while, but it is not necessarily a sign of strength. Rising delinquencies or shrinking savings buffers can mean the pattern is harder to maintain.

### 6. Pessimism can be a general habit

Surveys also reflect a tendency to describe "the economy" more negatively than "my own situation." Many people report feeling fine personally while worrying about the country at large.

## Where sentiment has been useful

It would be wrong to dismiss sentiment data. It has value in specific ways:

- **Inflation expectations.** What households expect can influence wage demands and pricing behavior, which is why central bankers monitor these questions.
- **Turning points.** Sharp, sustained deteriorations have at times appeared alongside slowdowns, particularly when job worries rise.
- **Distribution of views.** Breakdowns by income, age or region can show who is under pressure, even if the total looks stable.
- **Big-ticket intentions.** Plans to buy homes, cars or appliances can offer early clues about interest-rate-sensitive sectors.

## What to compare it against: hard spending data

To judge whether mood is translating into behavior, pair sentiment with measures of what people actually did:

| Indicator | What it shows | Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Census Bureau retail sales | Monthly sales at stores and online retailers | Reported in current dollars, so inflation can inflate the headline; revised often |
| Personal consumption expenditures (BEA) | Broader spending including services | Released with a lag and revised |
| Real (inflation-adjusted) spending | Whether people are buying more goods, not just paying more | Depends on the price index used |
| Card and payment data from banks and processors | Near-real-time transaction patterns | Reflects each firm's customer base, not the whole country |
| Employment and wage data | The income that supports spending | Strong jobs can coexist with weak sentiment |
| Savings rate and credit data | Whether spending is funded sustainably | Can change quickly |
| Company earnings commentary | What retailers say about traffic and trade-down | Each firm's view is partial |

## A practical way to read the two together

1. **Look at trends, not single months.** A three-month average of sentiment and spending is far less noisy than one release.
2. **Adjust for inflation.** Ask whether retail sales rose because people bought more or because prices rose.
3. **Check who is spending.** Look for splits between higher- and lower-income households and between goods and services.
4. **Watch the financial plumbing.** Rising credit card balances and delinquencies alongside strong spending suggest a different story than spending funded by income growth.
5. **Compare expectations questions with current-conditions questions.** They often diverge, and the difference can be informative.
6. **Treat surprises as questions, not conclusions.** A big gap between mood and spending is a prompt to investigate, not proof that either is wrong.

## The bottom line

Sentiment surveys capture how people feel and what they expect. Spending data captures what they do. Feelings and behavior often move together over long periods, but in the short run they can diverge for good reasons: prices are visible, spending is concentrated, opinions are colored by news, and routine purchases continue regardless of mood.

The most reliable approach is to avoid relying on any single number. Use sentiment as a window into worries and expectations, use hard spending data as a record of behavior, and look for where the two agree or disagree. That gap is often where the most interesting part of the economic story lies.

*This article is for general informational purposes only and is not financial, investment or economic advice. Data releases and survey methods change over time, so consult the original publishers for current figures and methodology.*

items.title: [Consumer Psychology #10] Why "Was $499, Now $299" Works on You: Framing, Anchoring, and Loss Aversion
items.body:
> We don't judge prices and offers in a vacuum. How a choice is worded, which number we see first, and whether we feel we're gaining or losing all shape what we buy.

## Today's Concept

Classic economics assumed shoppers act like calculators: they compare costs and benefits and pick the best deal. **Behavioral economics** studies what people actually do, and it finds predictable patterns that differ from that ideal. Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky did much of the founding work in the 1970s and '80s. Kahneman later won the Nobel Prize in economics for it.

Three of these patterns come up all the time in shopping:

**1. Framing: the same facts, described differently**
Two descriptions can carry the same information and still lead people to different choices. In one well-known study, people rated ground beef labeled "75% lean" more favorably than beef labeled "25% fat," even though the two labels mean the same thing. The frame tells us where to look. "Lean" points to the good part and "fat" points to the bad part.

**2. Anchoring: the first number sticks**
When we estimate a value, we tend to start from whatever number we saw first (the *anchor*) and then adjust, usually not far enough. In Tversky and Kahneman's experiments, even a number from a spinning wheel that was clearly random pulled people's later estimates toward it. In stores, the anchor is often the "original" price, the most expensive item on the menu, or a "suggested retail price."

**3. Loss aversion: losing hurts more than winning feels good**
Losing $50 usually feels worse than finding $50 feels good. Research estimates vary, but losses often carry roughly twice the psychological weight of equal gains. That's why marketers like phrases such as "Don't miss out," "Your cart is about to expire," and "You'll lose your rewards points."

None of these patterns means people are foolish. They are mental shortcuts that save effort most of the time. Marketers know about them, though, so it's worth noticing when they're being used on you.

## In Everyday Life

Picture a Black Friday ad for a 65-inch TV:

- **"Was $499, now $299!"** The $499 works as an anchor. Next to it, $299 looks like a steal, even if the TV rarely sold for $499. (The FTC has rules against fake "former prices," but a reference price shapes your judgment either way.)
- **"Save $200"** vs. **"40% off"** says the same thing in two frames. For pricier items, a dollar amount usually sounds bigger. For cheaper items, a percentage often does. Retailers tend to pick whichever frame looks larger.
- **"Only 3 left at this price. Deal ends at midnight."** This turns *not buying* into *losing* something. Now you aren't weighing a $299 purchase. You're trying not to lose $200 in savings.

A simple counter-move: before you look at the "was" price, ask yourself what the TV is worth to you and what it costs at two other retailers. That way you set your own anchor.

## 3-Line Summary

1. **Framing:** How information is worded ("75% lean" vs. "25% fat") changes choices even when the facts don't change.
2. **Anchoring:** The first number we see, like an "original price," pulls our sense of value toward it.
3. **Loss aversion:** Losses tend to feel about twice as strong as equal gains, so "don't miss out" messages work well.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**Q1.** A gym advertises "Members who skip a month lose their $100 sign-up credit." Which principle is it mainly using?
- (a) Anchoring
- (b) Loss aversion
- (c) Neither. It's just information.

**Q2. True or False:** An anchor only affects you if the number is clearly relevant to the decision.

**Q3.** A restaurant puts a $95 steak at the top of its menu, and most diners order the $38 dish instead. The $95 item is most likely working as:
- (a) A frame
- (b) An anchor
- (c) A loss

## 📚 Key Terms

- **Behavioral economics:** The study of how people actually make economic decisions, including predictable departures from purely "rational" choice.
- **Framing effect:** The tendency for choices to change based on how the same information is presented.
- **Anchoring:** Relying too heavily on the first number you see when estimating value.
- **Loss aversion:** The tendency to feel losses more strongly than gains of the same size.
- **Reference price:** The price a shopper compares an offer against, such as a "was" price or MSRP.

---

*Answers: Q1 (b). The message is built around losing something you already have, not around gaining a benefit. Q2 False. In Tversky and Kahneman's experiments, even clearly random numbers pulled people's estimates toward them. Q3 (b). The expensive item sets a high reference point, so the $38 dish seems reasonable next to it. This is sometimes called a "decoy" or "anchor" item.*

items.title: PCE vs. CPI: Why the Fed's Favorite Inflation Gauge Often Tells a Different Story
items.body:
As the Federal Reserve approaches its December policy meeting, one number gets more attention inside the central bank than almost any other: the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index. Most households know the Consumer Price Index (CPI) better. It drives the headlines, cost-of-living adjustments and everyday conversation about prices. Yet the Fed formally targets PCE inflation, and the two measures can point in different directions.

This explainer covers what each index measures, where they differ, and why the gap matters when you read the data.

## Two Gauges, Two Agencies

**CPI** is produced by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). It tracks the average change in prices that urban consumers pay out of pocket for a fixed basket of goods and services.

**PCE** is produced by the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) as part of the national income and product accounts. It measures price changes for the goods and services consumed by households. That includes spending made on their behalf.

Both aim to answer the question "how fast are prices rising?" But they start from different data and answer slightly different versions of the question.

## Difference 1: Weights

The most important difference is how much each category counts.

- **Housing.** Shelter makes up roughly a third of the overall CPI basket. In PCE its share is much smaller, often cited as around 15%. When rents and housing costs are the main driver of inflation, CPI tends to run hotter than PCE. When shelter cools, CPI can fall faster.
- **Health care.** PCE gives health care a larger weight. It counts spending by Medicare, Medicaid and employer-provided insurance, not only what consumers pay directly.
- **Other categories.** Items such as financial services and some services paid for by third parties have a bigger presence in PCE than in CPI.

Because the weights differ, the same price moves can produce different headline numbers.

## Difference 2: Scope

CPI is built from out-of-pocket spending by urban households. PCE covers a broader universe:

- Spending by all households, including rural ones
- Spending by nonprofit institutions serving households
- Costs paid by third parties, such as government health programs and employer-sponsored insurance

This is why health care looks so different in the two indexes. A hospital bill paid largely by an insurer shows up more fully in PCE than in CPI.

## Difference 3: Methodology

The two indexes also differ in how they are calculated.

- **Weight updates.** CPI weights come mainly from the Consumer Expenditure Survey and are updated on a set schedule. PCE weights come from broader business and national accounts data and are updated continuously.
- **Formula.** PCE uses a chained, Fisher-type formula that captures how consumers shift between goods when relative prices change. If beef gets expensive and shoppers buy more chicken, PCE reflects that substitution faster. CPI has narrowed this gap over the years, but it still captures substitution less fully.
- **Revisions.** CPI is almost never revised after release, apart from seasonal factors. PCE can be revised several times as new source data arrive, sometimes for months or years.

Together these differences have historically kept CPI inflation a few tenths of a percentage point above PCE inflation on average. The gap is not constant. It can widen or narrow depending on what is driving prices.

## Why the Fed Prefers PCE

The Fed adopted an explicit 2% inflation goal in 2012, measured by the PCE price index. Policymakers have given several reasons for preferring it:

1. **Broader coverage.** It captures a wider range of consumer spending.
2. **Better handling of substitution.** The formula adjusts as buying patterns change.
3. **Revisability.** Historical data can be corrected as better information becomes available.

Officials also watch **core PCE**, which excludes food and energy. These categories are volatile, and core readings are often seen as a cleaner guide to underlying trends. Many analysts also follow narrower cuts, such as core services excluding housing.

## Why the Two Can Point in Different Directions

Divergences usually come from a few sources:

- **A shelter-driven swing.** If rent and owners' equivalent rent move sharply, CPI reacts more because shelter has a larger weight.
- **Health care and financial services.** A jump in medical prices or portfolio-management fees, which often follow stock-market levels, can lift PCE more than CPI.
- **Revisions.** An updated PCE estimate can shift the picture after the first release.
- **Timing.** CPI is published first each month, and parts of it feed into PCE estimates. Markets often treat CPI and producer price data as a preview of PCE. Those previews are estimates, and the final PCE figure can differ.

## How to Read the Data

A few habits help when the two measures disagree:

- **Compare like with like.** Check whether you are looking at headline or core figures, and monthly or year-over-year changes.
- **Look at the drivers.** Find out which categories explain the gap before drawing conclusions.
- **Watch the trend, not one release.** A single month can be distorted by one-off factors.
- **Remember the purpose.** CPI is widely used for inflation-linked adjustments, including Social Security cost-of-living increases. PCE guides monetary policy.

## What It Means for the December Meeting

Policymakers weigh many inputs, including employment, wage growth, inflation expectations and financial conditions. PCE inflation, especially the core measure, is central to their assessment of whether prices are returning to the 2% goal. When CPI and PCE tell different stories, officials look past the headline numbers and examine the components behind them.

For readers, the takeaway is that neither index is "right" and the other "wrong." They measure related but distinct things. Knowing how they differ helps you interpret each new release and understand why the Fed's reading of inflation may not match the figure in the morning headline.

*This article is for general informational purposes only. It is not investment, financial or tax advice. Figures and weights described here are approximate and change over time. Check the BLS and BEA websites for current data and methodology.*
